newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea seeks to arrest two bankers over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: South Korea seeks to arrest two bankers over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors on Wednesday sought to arrest the heads of two leading banks, widening a probe into a scandal surrounding Hanbo Steel Co.

In a new twist to the unfolding saga, a prominent opposition member of parliament said he had taken money from Chung Tae-soo, founder of the steelmaker's parent company, Hanbo Group, partly to fund an election campaign.
Prosecutors last Friday arrested Chung on charges of fraud and violating laws on cheques and trust and savings companies.
"We filed with a court today a request for arrest warrants against Mr Sheen Kwang-shik and Woo Chan-mok," a prosecution official told Reuters.
Sheen is the president of Korea First Bank and Woo the head of Cho Hung Bank.
Prosecutors have been questioning Sheen, Woo and Lee Hyung-koo, former chief of the state-run Korea Development Bank, since they were summoned on Tuesday.
The official did not say whether the prosecution was considering any action against Lee.

The three banks are the main creditors of Hanbo Steel, which racked up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

Prosecution officials said on Tuesday the bankers would be questioned over whether they received commissions in return for offering huge loans to Hanbo Steel, the country's second largest steelmaker and flagship of the Hanbo Group.

Politician Kwon Roh-kap, a close associate of opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, told reporters he had accepted between 150 million and 160 million won ($173,000 and $184,000) from Hanbo founder Chung on three occasions since 1993.
Kim Dae-jung heads the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
Asked by reporters about the nature of the money, Kwon said: "I believe they were either political funds or rice cake money. But I have nothing to do with preferential lendings to Hanbo."
South Koreans traditionally swap small amounts of money, known as rice cake money, or gifts during major holidays as a token of friendship or respect.
Kwon said part of the money was used to finance a party election in 1993.

He is the first politician to admit taking money from Chung, who built up South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding the steelmaker and by acquiring or setting up 18 companies over the past three years.
State prosecutors have questioned officials of Hanbo and its creditor banks over a lobbying fund kept by Chung and examined the conglomerate's bank accounts to check for irregularities.
They said the bankers under interrogation were asked if they had faced any pressure from politicians or government officials over the loans.
With presidential elections only 10 months away, the Hanbo loan scandal has emerged as a sensitive political issue.
President Kim, who ordered a probe into the loans last week, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.
